claims.topic: Q1 JIT: change size vs deep models (SZZ labels)
claims.claim: On six projects with SZZ labels, a logistic regression on one feature, lines added (LApredict), had the best mean AUC. It beat DeepJIT, CC2Vec and the multi-feature traditional models. Because the model only ranks commits by lines added, its within-project and cross-project AUC are identical. In 10-fold CV on the training data, lines added alone scored slightly above all features combined. Deep models did not consistently beat the traditional ones.
claims.numbers: 310,370 commits, 81,300 SZZ-defective (8.64%-41.20% per project). LApredict mean AUC 0.7246 (per project 0.6757-0.7495). Mean AUC within/cross-project: DeepJIT 0.7065/0.6808, CC2Vec 0.7055/0.6771, LR-JIT 0.6726/0.6490, DBN-JIT 0.6847/0.6532. Lines added alone 0.7236 vs all features 0.7212 (CV). Deep models at least 81k x / 120k x slower than LApredict (train/test).
claims.source_title: Deep Just-in-Time Defect Prediction: How Far Are We? (Zeng, Zhang, Zhang, Zhang)

claims.topic: Q1 JIT: Kamei large-scale study, typical performance
claims.claim: A change-level logistic regression over 14 change measures, on 6 open-source and 5 commercial projects, predicts defect-inducing changes well above random. In the open-source projects the main risk-increasing factors were number of files, relative churn (LA/LT, LT/NF) and whether the change is a fix. In the commercial projects the size factors were consistently important.
claims.numbers: Average accuracy 68%, recall 64%, precision 34% (OSS 37%/67%, commercial 32%/62%). The text states an average AUC of 73% vs 50% for random. 20% of inspection effort finds 35% of defect-inducing changes. One commercial project had only 2.5% defect-inducing changes. The per-project AUC table is an image I could not read.
claims.source_title: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Just-in-Time Quality Assurance (Kamei et al.)

claims.topic: Q1 JIT: size baseline on better-validated labels
claims.claim: JIT-Defects4J builds labels from manually validated bug-fix lines (LLTC4J), traced back to the inducing commits, and uses a time-ordered 80/20 split. On it, the lines-added baseline LApredict had the lowest F1 and near-lowest AUC, and was clearly beaten by the semantic and deep models. The authors conclude that a simple supervised model does not capture what makes a commit defect-inducing.
claims.numbers: 21 Java projects, 27,319 commits, 2,332 defect-inducing (8.54%). AUC/F1: LApredict 0.694/0.059, Deeper 0.682/0.246, DeepJIT 0.775/0.293, CC2Vec 0.791/0.248, JITLine 0.802/0.261, JIT-Fine 0.881/0.431.
claims.source_title: The Best of Both Worlds: Integrating Semantic Features with Expert Features for Defect Prediction and Localization (Ni et al.)

claims.claim: Six fine-tuned pre-trained backbones (RoBERTa, CodeBERT, GPT2, CodeGPT, BART, PLBART) on the CC2Vec QT and OpenStack SZZ data roughly matched DeepJIT and CC2Vec in AUC; the gains were mostly in F1. With an untrained classification head ('zero-shot') the outputs were degenerate. No size-only baseline was reported.
claims.numbers: QT (25,704 commits, 7.1% defective): AUC DeepJIT 0.79, CC2Vec 0.81, pre-trained 0.81-0.82; F1 0.31-0.35 vs 0.27/0.23. OpenStack (13,304 commits, 12.2%): AUC DeepJIT 0.74, CC2Vec 0.76, pre-trained 0.79-0.81; F1 0.39-0.42. Trained on 2,000 samples: AUC 0.76-0.81. Zero-shot: accuracy and recall at 0 or 1, F1 undefined.
claims.source_title: A study on the impact of pre-trained model on Just-In-Time defect prediction (Guo et al.)

claims.topic: Q2 SZZ label noise: Herbold et al.
claims.claim: With manually validated issue types and links, about half of the commits SZZ marks as bug fixes are not bug fixes. SZZ's flagged bug-inducing commits contain roughly as many false as true ones, and the main cause is mislabelled issues rather than the blame step. With a six-month window, about one file is falsely labelled defective for each correct one, and two defective files are missed.
claims.numbers: 398 releases of 38 Apache projects. Linked BUG issues mislabelled: median 42.3%. SZZ recovers a median 92.4% of the true bug-inducing commits, with false positives equal to a median 92.7% (MAD 53.6%) of the true count. SZZ-RA recovers 100%, with 69.8% false positives. With validated issues (JLMIV), false positives fall to 12.1%. Bug-inducing commits are a median 5.2% of all commits.
claims.source_title: Problems with SZZ and features: An empirical study of the state of practice of defect prediction data collection (Herbold, Trautsch, Trautsch, Ledel)

claims.topic: Q2 SZZ label noise: developer-informed oracle
claims.claim: Against an oracle in which developers explicitly named the bug-inducing commit, the standard SZZ variants have precision 0.36-0.66, so 34-64% of the commits they flag are not the one the developer named. Recall is about 0.45-0.69 and the best F1 is 0.61 (R-SZZ).
claims.numbers: 1,930 instances. Precision/recall/F1 without date filter: B-SZZ 0.39/0.69/0.50, AG-SZZ 0.45/0.60/0.52, L-SZZ 0.52/0.45/0.48, R-SZZ 0.66/0.57/0.61, MA-SZZ 0.36/0.64/0.46, PyDriller 0.39/0.67/0.49, SZZ Unleashed 0.09/0.72/0.16. With the issue-date filter, R-SZZ precision is 0.73 and F1 0.64.
claims.source_title: Evaluating SZZ Implementations Through a Developer-informed Oracle (Rosa et al.)

claims.topic: Q2 SZZ label noise: da Costa framework
claims.claim: With no ground truth available, the authors applied three plausibility criteria to five SZZ implementations on ten Apache projects. Many of the reported bug-introducing changes are implausible, and the proposed SZZ refinements increased disagreement with the affected versions developers recorded.
claims.numbers: 32,033 bug fixes (2,637 with affected-version data). Disagreement ratio: B-SZZ 0-9%, MA-SZZ 0-17%, L-SZZ 6-29%, R-SZZ 24-50%. Bugs whose inducing changes span more than a year: B-SZZ 65%, MA-SZZ 46%. 45% of B-SZZ inducing changes lead to multiple future bugs. Manual check: 38 of 60 upper-extreme MA-SZZ entries were suspicious vs 1 of 60 at the lower extreme.
claims.source_title: A Framework for Evaluating the Results of the SZZ Approach for Identifying Bug-Introducing Changes (da Costa et al.)

claims.topic: Q2 SZZ label noise: Linux kernel Fixes-tag oracle
claims.claim: On the Linux kernel, with developers' 'Fixes:' tags as the oracle, six SZZ variants reach precision 0.40-0.59 and recall 0.43-0.58. 17.47% of the fixes are 'ghost commits' that SZZ cannot trace.
claims.numbers: 76,046 fix/inducing pairs (Oct 2013 to Nov 2022). 81% (317 of 383) of sampled tags were judged clearly correct. P/R/F1: B-SZZ 0.42/0.58/0.49, AG-SZZ 0.42/0.56/0.48, L-SZZ 0.57/0.43/0.49, R-SZZ 0.59/0.45/0.51, MA-SZZ 0.40/0.55/0.46, PyDriller 0.43/0.55/0.48.
claims.source_title: Evaluating SZZ Implementations: An Empirical Study on the Linux Kernel (Lyu, Kang, Widyasari, Lawall, Lo)

claims.topic: Q2 SZZ label noise: manually traced bug origins
claims.claim: The authors manually traced how 116 bugs were introduced in two projects. SZZ-based algorithms were not very accurate, and when every commit SZZ flags is counted, about two-thirds of them are false positives.
claims.numbers: F-score 0.44-0.77; true positives never above 63%. Precision under the SZZ 'All' criterion: 0.32 (Nova), 0.31 (ElasticSearch). Best case (SZZ-1, 'At least' criterion): precision 0.71/0.75, F-score 0.76/0.77.
claims.source_title: How bugs are born: a model to identify how bugs are introduced in software components (Rodriguez-Perez et al.)

claims.topic: Q3 LMs on realistic vulnerability detection: PrimeVul
claims.claim: On a realistic, deduplicated, better-labelled benchmark, code LM performance collapses compared with older benchmarks. In the paired evaluation (vulnerable function vs its patched version), no model, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 included, beat a random guess; the authors call this performance no better than random.
claims.numbers: StarCoder2 F1 68.26% on BigVul vs 3.09% on PrimeVul (18.05% when trained on PrimeVul). Pair-wise correct (P-C): fine-tuned code LMs 1.06-3.01%; GPT-3.5 two-shot 5.67%, CoT 6.21%, fine-tuned 1.24%; GPT-4 two-shot 5.14%, CoT 12.94%; random guess 22.70%. VD-S (FNR at FPR <= 0.5%) about 89-92% on PrimeVul. Label accuracy: BigVul 25%, CVEFixes 51.7%, DiverseVul 60%, PrimeVul 86-92%. Prior test sets had up to 18.9% leakage from training. PrimeVul has 6,968 vulnerable and 228,800 benign functions and 5,480 pairs.
claims.source_title: Vulnerability Detection with Code Language Models: How Far Are We? (Ding et al.)
claims.quote: akin to random guessing in the most stringent settings

claims.topic: Q3 LLMs on vulnerability detection: SecLLMHolmes
claims.claim: Eight LLMs tested on 228 code scenarios along eight dimensions gave non-deterministic answers and incorrect or unfaithful reasoning. All had high false-positive rates and flagged patched code as still vulnerable. They did poorly on real-world CVEs, and trivial renames or added library calls flipped their answers.
claims.numbers: Wrong answers after trivial augmentations: 26% of cases (PaLM2), 17% (GPT-4). Best accuracy on the hand-crafted scenarios: GPT-4, 89.5% with its best prompt. The real-world set has vulnerable and patched versions of 15 CVEs, and every LLM was wrong on several.
claims.source_title: LLMs Cannot Reliably Identify and Reason About Security Vulnerabilities (Yet?): A Comprehensive Evaluation, Framework, and Benchmarks (Ullah et al.)

claims.topic: Q3/Q4 code LMs on high-confidence JIT labels: ReDef
claims.claim: ReDef is a function-level JIT dataset whose defective labels are anchored on reverts. Fine-tuned code LMs reach only modest F1 and zero-shot Qwen2.5-7B does worse. Counterfactual perturbations (swapping added and deleted blocks, reversing the diff) barely change performance. The authors read this as reliance on superficial cues ('semantic blindness') rather than understanding of the change.
claims.numbers: 22 C/C++ projects; 3,164 defective and 10,268 clean (about 24% defective); label precision 0.92 on a 100-sample audit. Best fine-tuned F1: CodeBERT 0.397 (PR-AUC 0.324-0.335), CodeT5+ 0.377, UniXcoder 0.376, Qwen2.5-7B with LoRA 0.354; precision 0.25-0.31. Zero-shot Qwen2.5-7B: F1 0.028-0.344 depending on encoding, precision 0.23-0.26. F1 change under perturbation: -3.56% to +0.48%.
claims.source_title: ReDef: Do Code Language Models Truly Understand Code Changes for Just-in-Time Software Defect Prediction? (Nam, Kim, Ryu, Baik)

claims.topic: Q4 LLMs vs metric baseline on diff risk: Meta DRS
claims.claim: Meta labels diffs that caused production incidents (SEVs, 0.17% of test diffs) and uses a production logistic regression as the baseline. Its features cover diff size relative to the file, number of files and authors, criticality, complexity and author expertise. LLM embeddings fed to a classifier without fine-tuning captured fewer SEVs than this baseline. Only the fine-tuned ('risk-aligned') LLMs beat it, and mainly at the strict gating levels.
claims.numbers: Train 855,282 diffs; test 181,052 diffs with 305 SEVs. SEVs captured when gating 5%/10%/50%: LR 18.7%/27.9%/84.6%. Relative to LR: StarBERT 0.61x/0.85x/0.81x; iCodeLlama-34B embeddings 0.58x/0.65x/0.82x; iDiffLlama-13B embeddings 0.65x/0.81x/0.90x; iCodeLlama-34B risk-aligned 1.26x/1.28x/0.98x; iDiffLlama-13B risk-aligned 1.40x/1.52x/1.05x (26.2%/42.3%/88.5%). In a second organisation: LR 11.9%/26.3%/84.4% vs 21.9%/39.4%/88.8%. No AUC is reported.
claims.source_title: Moving Faster and Reducing Risk: Using LLMs in Release Deployment (Abreu et al., Meta)

claims.topic: Q4 fine-tuned LLM on SZZ-labelled JIT data: DRS-OSS
claims.claim: A Llama 3.1 8B model fine-tuned with QLoRA on ApacheJIT, using a chronological 80/10/10 split, gave the best F1 and AUC among the baselines it compared. Its input includes the commit message, the diff, and change metrics (size, entropy, files touched) as special tokens. No size-only or zero-shot baseline was reported.
claims.numbers: F1 0.641, ROC-AUC 0.895, precision 0.491, recall 0.84. F1/AUC of baselines: CodeReviewer 0.622/0.815, JITGNN 0.5/0.81, NeuroJIT 0.56/0.8. Recall at top 5% / 10% / 30%: 0.315 / 0.503 / 0.864.
claims.source_title: DRS-OSS: Practical Diff Risk Scoring with LLMs (Sayedsalehi, Rigby, Mockus)

claims.topic: Q4 fine-tuned vs zero-shot closed LLMs on JIT-DP
claims.claim: The study compares encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder code LMs, fine-tuned open models against zero-shot prompted closed LLMs (GPT models, Gemini), on JIT-Defects4J. Fine-tuned small and medium open models significantly outperform zero-shot closed LLMs, and CodeT5+ and UniXcoder beat the prior state of the art cross-project.
claims.numbers: Fine-tuned results as summarised by the same authors (CodeFlowLM, arXiv 2512.00231, Table 6): UniXcoder ROC-AUC 0.901, F1 0.519; CodeT5+ 0.899/0.519; JIT-Smart baseline 0.885/0.486. The zero-shot closed-LLM AUC/F1 values are in the paywalled chapter and I could not see them.
claims.source_title: Pre-trained Code Language Models for Just-in-Time Software Defect Prediction: An Empirical Study (Monteiro, Cabral, de Oliveira)

claims.topic: Q4 zero-/few-shot LLM change-risk prediction: Prime Video
claims.claim: Risky commits are those linked to incident reviews, at a 1:19 ratio, and the study also uses an ApacheJIT subsample. Prompting Claude Sonnet 3.7 or 4.5 zero- or few-shot with the diff, description and extracted features gave low F1, far below a feature-based XGBoost. The authors call the change-volume metrics (lines added/deleted) noisy, although volume-only XGBoost still scored F1 0.565 (vs 0.809 for code-complexity features only). Evaluation was 10-fold CV with threshold 0.2, and no AUC is reported.
claims.numbers: Prime Video (149 risky / 2,831 safe), P/R/F1: Sonnet 3.7 zero-shot 0.087/0.641/0.153, few-shot 0.137/0.615/0.216; Sonnet 4.5 zero-shot 0.135/0.792/0.231, few-shot 0.157/0.779/0.261. ApacheJIT (2,980-commit stratified subsample, 5% positive): F1 Sonnet 3.7 zero-shot 0.175, few-shot 0.204; Sonnet 4.5 zero-shot 0.230, few-shot 0.222. XGBoost F1 0.846 (Prime Video) / 0.771 (ApacheJIT, 22,300 commits); logistic regression baseline 0.145/0.158.
claims.source_title: Deployment Risk Assessment Using Diff-Aware Features: A Case Study at Prime Video (Kurup et al.)

literature.summary: Not out of line. On SZZ labels, size alone typically gives AUC 0.68-0.75 (LApredict per project; 0.694 on JIT-Defects4J), so 0.67 is normal. SZZ labels are noisy: precision against developer-confirmed oracles is 0.36-0.66 (Rosa) and 0.40-0.59 (Linux), and Herbold finds roughly as many false as true inducing commits. Zero-shot LLMs are weak on realistic code-defect tasks. On PrimeVul pairs every model scores below a random guess. Zero-shot Claude reaches F1 0.15-0.23 at 5% prevalence, zero-shot Qwen's precision is near the base rate, and untuned LLM embeddings trail Meta's metric-based regression. Only supervised models beat size, and not always (JIT-Fine 0.881 vs 0.694; Zeng: no gain). No study reports zero-shot AUC at matched size; ~0.51 matches the paired and perturbation results.
